title: Banks: Home loan stress climbs as ANZ posts $7.6b profit
full_text:
ANZ Bank chief executive Nuno Matos says late repayments on home loans have ticked up as the bank reported annual cash profit of $7.6 billion.
Yesterday, ANZ announced its profit for the year to September jumped 31 per cent after last year's result was dragged down by charges from a cost-cutting drive.
ANZ said that if these "significant items" were excluded, its cash profits for the year rose 10 per cent.
The bank's net interest margin - a key measure of profitability - was unchanged at 1.53 per cent, as the benefits from higher official interest rates were offset by competition in the home loan market.
The results showed ANZ's bottom line benefited from a 14 per cent decline in operating expenses, while its operating income rose 3 per cent.
Provisions for bad and doubtful debts increased by 32 per cent to $582 million.
Matos said the global backdrop had become more volatile in the past year, pointing to rising oil prices, geopolitical tensions and the artificial intelligence boom.
He said ANZ's retail customers were "largely resilient" with 87 per cent ahead on their repayments and 75 per cent maintaining savings buffers of at least three months.
"However, we acknowledge that some customers are experiencing financial pressures, which has been more evident in the second half," he said. "The economic backdrop of Australia ... is a more challenging one, let's be clear. So undoubtedly, Australia is going to weather a less benign environment."
The bank is forecasting economic growth of no more than 2 per cent this year with a mid-range scenario of 1.6 per cent which Matos said was "certainly a modest growth." However, Matos said there was also a "super cycle of investment" with governments looking to fund budget deficits and competing for long-term capital with investors looking to fund renewables, defence and AI projects.
"We are in a world, from a funding perspective, with so many projects going on," he said. "It's a tough situation which is creating inflation and higher rates."
ANZ chief financial officer Farhan Faruqui said while non-performing exposures were flat over the year, there had been an increase in the second half, primarily driven by its Australian mortgage portfolio, reflecting higher cost of living and interest rate pressures on customers.
"Our 90-day plus delinquencies increased by 12 basis points to 95 basis points over the last six months, with a small increase in hardship assistance," he said, but noted individual provision losses remained low at $8 million for the half supported by strong collateral coverage.
"Competition for capital to fund data centres, government spending and the energy transition has intensified, with this expenditure super-cycle, combined with inflationary supply side shocks, driving interest rates higher globally. Against this backdrop, the economies across our geographic footprint remain relatively resilient."
ANZ's small business portfolio delinquencies remained steady at 2.2 per cent over the second half of the year, however Faruqui noted "some emerging stress" in the agriculture and transport and logistics portfolios, reflecting the higher cost operating environment.
He said the bank was maintaining a "prudent approach" by increasing its collective provisions in the second half, accounting for the impact of the evolving economic and geopolitical environment, including the impact of elevated inflation and interest rates.
Citi head of Australian bank research Thomas Strong said ANZ's results beat consensus expectations, driven by lower bad debts and better cost control than expected.
The bank announced a final dividend of 83¢ a share, with franking increased from 70 per cent to 80 per cent.
